group.passage: Today, most of us do math on a phone. Long before phones, however, people used much simpler tools. Below are a sign from the math exhibit at a city museum and a report that a high school student wrote after she visited the exhibit.

passage_parts.label: A
passage_parts.title: Museum Sign: The Abacus
passage_parts.text: This wooden frame is an abacus, one of the oldest counting tools in the world. Small beads slide along thin rods. Each rod stands for a place value, such as ones, tens, or hundreds. A bar divides the frame into two parts. On a Chinese abacus, every rod has two beads above the bar and five below it. Each upper bead is worth five, and each lower bead is worth one. To add, the user pushes beads toward the bar. To subtract, the user moves them away from it. For hundreds of years, shopkeepers and traders across Asia did their daily math this way, and in skilled hands, the tool can be surprisingly fast. Best of all, it needs no batteries, and there is nothing to plug in. It keeps working even when the lights go out.

passage_parts.label: B
passage_parts.title: Student Report: From Beads to Buttons
passage_parts.text: After my visit, I wanted to know how calculators took the place of the abacus. The first electronic calculators appeared in the early 1960s. They sat on office desks, and they were heavy and expensive, so few families could afford one. Then, in the early 1970s, small pocket models reached stores. They ran on batteries, and they could add, subtract, multiply, and divide at the press of a button. At first they still cost a lot, but their prices kept falling. Within a few years, many students owned one, and students still use them in math class today. However, the abacus has not disappeared. In some parts of Asia, children still take abacus classes. After years of practice, some of them can do math without the tool at all. They simply picture the beads in their minds and move them there.

translation_zh.text:
【引言】今天，我們大多數人用手機算數學。但在有手機很久以前，人們用的是簡單得多的工具。以下是市立博物館數學展的一塊展板，以及一位高中生參觀展覽後寫的報告。
【A 博物館展板：算盤】這個木框就是算盤，是世界上最古老的計算工具之一。小珠子沿著細細的桿子滑動，每一根桿子代表一個位值，例如個位、十位或百位。一根橫樑把木框分成兩部分。在中國算盤上，每根桿子橫樑上方有兩顆珠子、下方有五顆。上面每顆珠子代表五，下面每顆珠子代表一。做加法時，使用者把珠子往橫樑撥；做減法時，就把珠子撥離橫樑。幾百年來，亞洲各地的店主和商人都用這種方式處理每天的計算；在熟練的人手中，這個工具可以快得驚人。最棒的是，它不需要電池，也沒有任何東西要插電。就算停電了，它照樣能用。
【B 學生報告：從珠子到按鈕】參觀之後，我想知道計算機是怎麼取代算盤的。最早的電子計算機出現在 1960 年代初期。它們放在辦公桌上，又重又貴，所以很少家庭買得起。後來在 1970 年代初期，小型的口袋型計算機上市了。它們靠電池運作，按一個鍵就能加、減、乘、除。一開始它們還是很貴，但價格一路下跌，幾年之內，很多學生都有了一台，今天學生在數學課上也還在用。不過，算盤並沒有消失。在亞洲某些地方，孩子們仍然去上算盤課。經過多年練習，有些孩子甚至完全不用算盤也能計算：他們只要在腦海中想像珠子，在腦中撥動它們就行了。
